Draw weeks 13 to 28: kicking, fingerprints, hearing.
Draw weeks 29 to 40 and birth. Show the scroll to someone and explain it.

projects.record: Your finished scroll, and a photo of you explaining it.
projects.context: This 3-day project makes a long paper scroll, one mark for each of the 40 weeks a baby grows in the womb. You draw what happens week by week.

setup.art: A long paper scroll unrolled on the floor with 40 small marks along it, a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll out the paper. Mark 40 weeks, 5 centimetres apart.

setup.art: The first part of the scroll with drawings of one cell, a ball of cells, a beating heart and tiny fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what happens in each part of the 40 weeks.

setup.art: A child holding up a long scroll for a grandmother to see, pointing at the newborn at the end.
setup.caption: 3. Show your finished scroll to someone, and explain it.

flow.do: 1. Mark 40 weeks along the scroll, 5 centimetres apart. 2. Draw week 1, one cell. 3. Week 2, a ball of cells. 4. Week 6, a beating heart. 5. Week 8, a raspberry-sized embryo. 6. Week 12, fingers and toes.
flow.say: In the first three months, all the main body parts form. The baby is still very small. Let's draw it.
flow.kid: Mark 40 weeks. Draw one cell at week 1. Draw a heart at week 6. Draw fingers at week 12.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You mark the 40 weeks and draw the first three months of growing.

flow.do: Draw weeks 13 to 28: week 16, fingerprints forming. Week 18, first kicks the mother feels. Week 20, halfway, banana-sized. Week 24, hearing sounds. Week 28, eyes opening.
flow.say: In the middle months, the baby moves a lot. It starts to hear. Its fingerprints form.
flow.kid: Draw the middle months. Fingerprints at week 16. Kicks at week 18. Hearing at week 24.

check.q: On the scroll, which of these happens first?
check.why: The heart starts beating at about six weeks, very early. Hearing comes at about six months. Getting chubby happens in the last months. Picking 'hears sounds' first often means thinking the senses come first. In fact the heart and body parts come first.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You draw what happens to the baby in weeks 13 to 28.

flow.do: 1. Draw weeks 29 to 40: getting chubby, head turning down. 2. Draw birth at the very end. 3. Show the scroll to a family member and explain it.
flow.say: In the last months, the baby grows big and fat, and its lungs get ready. Then comes birth. Now tell someone the whole story.
flow.kid: Draw the last months and birth. Then show your scroll to someone. Tell them the story.

ask.q: Tell the story of the scroll from start to end.
good: It starts as one cell, splits into many, the heart beats, fingers form, it kicks and hears, gets big, and is born.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You finish the last months and birth, and explain your scroll.

challenges.title: The Egg-Baby Carrier
challenges.problem: Design a carrier that keeps a raw egg 'baby' safe and warm while you walk up and down the stairs twice.
constraints: You can only use things from home.
The carrier must be small enough to hold in one hand.
You must be able to look at the egg without taking it out.
materials: cotton, cloth, water, rice or newspaper
general: Pad the egg all round with cotton or cloth, so it cannot bang the sides.
Fill a small bottle with water and float the egg inside it, like a baby in the womb.
Wrap the carrier in a cloth to keep the warmth in.
creative: Make a bag within a bag, like the womb inside the mother's tummy.
Hang the egg in the middle of a box on stretchy rubber bands, so it bounces gently.
Use a ball of soft dough around the egg, like a thick cushion.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own carrier. Draw it first. Then build it, test it on the stairs, and check the egg. What would you change?

setup.caption: 1. Collect your materials and a raw egg.

setup.art: A child holding a small bottle of water with an egg floating in it, wrapped in a cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Build a carrier that cushions and warms the egg.

setup.caption: 3. Walk the stairs twice. Is the egg still whole?

flow.do: Talk about how the womb keeps a baby safe.
flow.say: A baby in the womb is protected by water, by the soft womb, and by the mother's body around it. How can we use those ideas?
flow.kid: How does the womb keep a baby safe? Use those ideas for your egg.

ask.q: What protects a baby in the womb?
good: The water around it.
The soft, stretchy womb.
The mother's body and tummy muscles.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Egg-Baby Carrier challenge. You think about how the womb protects a baby.

flow.kid: Draw your carrier. Then build it.

flow.kid: Walk the stairs twice. Then look at the egg. Is it whole?

Make the box out of thinner paper

challenges.title: Hold My Head! A safe baby sling

a doll or a soft toy, or a rolled towel
a grown-up to help tie it

Hold the doll upright against the chest, tummy to tummy.
Pull a fold of cloth up behind the doll's head.
creative: Look at how grandmothers and village women in India carry babies on their hip or back with a sari.
Make a pocket in the cloth for the doll's bottom, like a kangaroo's pouch.
Add a rolled towel as a head cushion.

items.p: How did every person begin?
opts: As a seed swallowed by the mother
items.why: Every person began as one cell, made when a cell from each parent joined. Picking 'a tiny ready-made baby' is an old idea scientists gave up. The body parts form step by step.

items.p: What does one cell do to make more cells?
opts: It stays the same for nine months
items.why: A cell splits into two, then each of those splits again. Picking 'eats other cells' mixes it up with how some germs are fought by the body.

items.p: A cell splits into 2, then 4, then 8, then ____.
items.why: Each time, every cell splits, so the number doubles. 8 doubled is 16.

items.p: Where does a baby grow before it is born?
items.why: A baby grows in the womb, a stretchy bag of muscle below the stomach. Picking 'stomach' is very common, because people say 'a baby in her tummy'. But the stomach is where food goes.

items.p: How does a baby in the womb get food and oxygen?
opts: Through the umbilical cord, from the mother's blood
By breathing air through its nose
items.why: The mother's blood brings food and oxygen to the placenta. The cord carries them to the baby. Picking 'breathing air' forgets that the baby is in water, with no air to breathe.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
pairs: the stretchy bag where the baby grows
passes food and oxygen from the mother's blood
the tube joining the baby to the placenta
the warm water the baby floats in
items.why: Each part has one main job. Together they keep the baby fed, safe and warm.
items.art: A simple labelled drawing of a baby in the womb.

items.p: The baby floats in warm water inside the womb.
items.why: True. This water, called amniotic fluid, cushions the baby and keeps it warm.

items.p: Remember the Floating Safe test, with a raw egg in an empty jar and in a jar full of water? Which egg usually stayed whole?
opts: The egg in the jar full of water
The egg in the empty jar
items.why: The water spreads out each bump, so the egg is hardly jolted. This is what the water around a baby does. Picking the empty jar often means thinking water is too heavy. But it presses gently all round.

items.p: A human baby usually grows in the womb for about ____ months.
items.why: About nine months, or 40 weeks.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items.why: One cell splits into a ball of cells. The heart beats at about six weeks. Fingers and toes form by twelve weeks. Hearing comes at about six months. Birth comes at about nine months.

items.p: What happens right after a baby is born?
opts: It takes its first breath of air
items.why: The first thing a newborn does is breathe air, often with a cry. Walking takes about a year and talking longer.

items.p: When the cord is cut and the stump falls off, it leaves the ____.
items.why: Your belly button is where your cord once joined you to the placenta.

items.p: Cutting the umbilical cord hurts the baby.
items.why: False. The cord has no nerves, so cutting it does not hurt the baby.

items.p: Sort these. Can a baby do this before it is born, or only after?
items.why: Babies in the womb move, suck, hiccup and hear. They cannot breathe air or drink milk until they are born.

items.p: Every family is made the same way.
items.why: False. Families are made in many ways: by birth, by adoption, by grandparents raising children, and more. But every person began as one cell, and grew in a womb.

items.p: Draw a baby in the womb. Label the womb, the water, the cord and the placenta.
items.a: A curled baby inside a round womb, surrounded by water, with a cord running from its tummy to a round placenta on the womb wall.
items.why: A good drawing shows the cord joined at the baby's tummy, and the placenta on the wall of the womb.
items.art: An empty oval outline for the child to draw in.

items.p: Every cell in your body has the same DNA, the same instruction book. Why are skin cells and heart cells so different?
opts: Each kind of cell reads different pages of the instructions
items.why: Every cell has the same instructions, but each kind uses different parts of them. Picking 'different DNA' is a very common idea. But almost every cell in your body has the same DNA.

items.p: The mother's blood and the baby's blood...
opts: stay mostly apart, with a thin wall between them
are always the same blood group
items.why: In the placenta, the two bloods come very close, with a thin wall between them. Food and oxygen pass through the wall. Picking 'mix freely' is common, but the bloods stay mostly apart. Babies can even have a different blood group.

items.p: Why does a baby in the womb hear low sounds best?
opts: Low sounds travel through water and bodies better than high sounds
The baby can see the sounds
items.why: Low sounds pass through water and the body well. High sounds get muffled. You may have found this in the Hearing Through Water test.

items.p: A newborn sees best at about 20 to 30 ____ away.
items.why: About 20 to 30 centimetres. That is the distance to the face of the person holding the baby.

items.p: A mother's thoughts can change the shape of her baby's ears.
items.why: False. This is an old belief. Thoughts do not travel to the baby. Only things in the blood, like food and medicines, reach it.

items.p: Your fingerprints formed before you were born, and their pattern never changes.
items.why: True. They form at about four months in the womb. They get bigger as you grow, but the pattern stays the same.

items.p: Why are a baby's skull bones not joined at birth?
opts: So the head can squeeze safely through at birth, and the brain can keep growing
Because bones are made after birth
So the baby can hear better
items.why: Soft gaps between the skull bones let the head change shape a little at birth. They also leave room for the brain to grow. They join up over the first two years.

items.p: At birth, the womb's muscles squeeze again and again. What are these squeezes called?
items.why: Contractions are squeezes of the womb's muscles. They slowly push the baby out. Hiccups and kicks are things the baby does.

items.p: A baby born by caesarean birth is born just as much as any other baby.
items.why: True. In a caesarean birth, doctors lift the baby out through a cut in the tummy. It is another way of being born.

items.p: Match each animal to about how long its baby grows inside the mother.
items.why: Bigger animals usually grow longer before birth. An elephant baby grows for almost two years.

items.p: Remember Keep the Baby Warm, with three bottles of warm water? Why did the bottle held on a chest stay warmest?
items.a: A person's body is always warm, so it keeps giving heat to the bottle. The cloth on top holds the heat in. The bottle alone lost heat to the air.
items.why: Warm bodies keep adding heat. This is why kangaroo care helps tiny babies.

items.p: Why can't a baby in the womb breathe air?
items.a: Because it is floating in water inside the womb, and there is no air there. It gets oxygen from its mother's blood instead, through the cord.
items.why: The baby's lungs are full of fluid until birth. Its oxygen comes through the cord.

items.p: Sort these. Does it reach the baby through the mother's blood, or not?
items.why: Things carried in the blood, like food, oxygen and some medicines, cross into the baby. Thoughts and pictures do not. This is why doctors ask pregnant mothers to eat well and check medicines.

items.p: Label the picture: womb, placenta, cord, water, baby.
items.why: The baby floats in water inside the womb. The cord joins its tummy to the placenta on the womb wall.
items.art: A simple drawing of a baby in the womb with five empty label lines.

items.p: Why do you think every person has a belly button?
items.a: Because everyone was once joined to a placenta by a cord, before they were born. When the cord was cut, it left the belly button.
items.why: Every person who was born grew in a womb, fed through a cord. The belly button is the mark it left.

items.p: Draw what you think one cell looks like, and then what it looks like after splitting four times.
items.a: One circle, then 2, then 4, then 8, then 16 circles.
items.why: Each split doubles the number. After four splits there are 16 cells.

items.p: A grown-up has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. Where did they all come from?
opts: From one first cell, splitting again and again
From the food, which turned into cells by itself
Each part of the body was made separately by the mother
items.why: Every cell came from the first one, by splitting. Food gives the building material, but cells only come from other cells. Picking 'from food by itself' mixes up building material with the builders.

items.p: If you start with 1 cell and every cell splits once a day, how many cells will there be after 10 days? Show your working.
items.why: Doubling grows very fast. Real cells do not all split at the same speed, but the idea is the same.

items.p: Some scientists think human babies are born early because the mother's hips are narrow. Others think it is because the mother's body runs out of energy to feed the baby. What does this tell us?
opts: Scientists still argue about why human babies are born so helpless
Scientists know the answer for sure
Babies are born early because they are tired
Nobody has ever asked the question
items.why: This is an open, debated question. Two good ideas compete, and scientists are still collecting evidence.

items.p: A few of the baby's cells can stay in the mother's body for many years after birth.
items.why: True. Scientists have found a son's cells in his mother's blood 27 years after his birth. Nobody yet knows exactly what these cells do.

items.p: Every cell has the same DNA. How do you think a cell knows whether to become a toe or an eye?
items.a: A good answer: the cells send each other chemical messages. A cell can tell where it is from how strong a message is around it. Then it reads the right part of its instructions.
items.why: This is still being worked out by scientists. Any thoughtful answer that mentions messages between cells, or where the cell is, shows good thinking.

items.p: Is a person the same person as the cell they began as? Give a reason for yes and a reason for no.
items.a: Yes: you grew from that cell without stopping, so it was the start of you. No: that cell had none of your memories and no body like yours, so it was very different from you now.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason on each side.

items.p: Before about 1950, nobody could see a baby inside the womb. Which invention changed that?
items.why: Ultrasound uses sounds too high to hear. They bounce off the baby and make a picture. Ian Donald, a Scottish doctor, published the first use of it for pregnancy in 1958.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: invented a quick score to check newborns at one and five minutes, in 1952
one of the first Indian women to qualify as a doctor, in 1886, after losing her own newborn son
Karl Ernst von Baer, an Estonian-German scientist
showed that babies form step by step from layers of cells, in the 1820s
items.why: Each one changed how we understand or care for babies. Anandibai Joshi wanted to help Indian mothers and babies after her own baby died at ten days old.

items.p: Why might it be good for a newborn to see best at about 25 centimetres?
items.a: That is the distance to the face of the person holding it. So the baby sees the faces of the people who feed and care for it, and starts to learn them.
items.why: Seeing close faces helps a baby bond with the people who look after it.

items.p: Why does a calf walk within an hour, but a human baby takes about a year?
opts: Human babies are born with brains and bodies that still have a lot of growing to do
Human babies do not need to walk
items.why: A human newborn's brain is only about a quarter of its grown-up size. Much of its growing happens after birth. That is why human children need care for so long.

items.p: An adopted child began life in a different way from other children.
items.why: False. Every person, adopted or not, began as one cell and grew in a womb. Adoption is about which family raises and loves a child, not about how the child began.

items.p: The food a mother eats becomes part of her baby. Trace a grain of rice back as far as you can, to where its atoms came from.
items.a: The grain came from a rice plant. The plant built it from air, water and soil, using sunlight. The atoms in the soil and air came from the Earth. Most of the Earth's atoms, apart from hydrogen, were made inside stars long ago.
items.why: This shows that a baby is built from the whole world: food, sun, soil and even stars.

items.p: Put these sizes in order from smallest to biggest.
items: a grain of rice, the size at 6 weeks
a raspberry, the size at 8 weeks
a banana, the size at 20 weeks
items.why: The first cell is about as wide as a hair. Then the baby grows from rice-sized to raspberry-sized to banana-sized, and then to about 50 centimetres at birth.

items.p: Is it fair that some babies are born near good hospitals and some are not? What could people do?
items.a: A thoughtful answer. For example: it is not fair, because every baby should be safe. People could train more midwives and nurses, build health centres in villages, and make sure every mother can get to a doctor.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a reason and an idea for helping.

items.p: Design a safe carrier for an egg-baby. Label two features that copy how the womb protects a baby.
items.a: Good features: water or padding all round the egg, a soft stretchy inner layer, a warm outer wrap.
items.why: The womb protects a baby with water, a soft muscle wall and the warm body around it.

items.p: Scientists completely understand how every cell knows where to go and what to become.
items.why: False. They understand a lot, like chemical messages between cells. But how millions of cells fit together into a whole body is still being worked out.

quiz.why: Everyone began as one cell, made from a cell from each parent. Picking 'a tiny ready-made baby' is an old idea. Body parts form step by step.

quiz.p: One cell splits into two. Each of those splits. Then each of those splits. How many cells now?
quiz.why: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. Each split doubles the number. Picking 3 means counting the splits, not the cells.

quiz.p: Every cell has the same instructions. Why do some become skin and some become bone?
opts: They read different parts of the instructions
quiz.why: Each kind of cell uses different parts of the same DNA. Picking 'different instructions' is a common idea, but almost every cell has the same DNA.
In the womb, a stretchy bag of muscle. Picking 'stomach' is common because we say 'tummy'. But the stomach is for food.

quiz.p: What does the umbilical cord do?
opts: Carries food and oxygen to the baby
Pulls the baby out at birth
quiz.why: The cord joins the baby to the placenta and carries food and oxygen. Picking 'pulls the baby out' mixes it up with birth, when the womb squeezes.

quiz.p: Remember the Floating Safe test with two raw eggs in jars? What did the water show?
opts: Water cushions bumps, like the water around a baby
Water makes eggs heavier and crack
quiz.why: The egg in water was protected because water spreads out each bump. This is what amniotic fluid does for a baby.

quiz.p: About how long does a human baby grow in the womb?
quiz.why: About nine months, or 40 weeks. Picking 2 years mixes it up with an elephant, whose baby grows for almost two years.

quiz.p: Which comes first as a baby grows?
quiz.why: The heart beats at about six weeks. Hearing comes at about six months. Getting chubby is in the last months.

quiz.p: What does a newborn baby do first?
quiz.why: The first breath comes right after birth. Before that the baby got oxygen through the cord.

opts: The place where your cord once joined you
A button that holds your skin on
quiz.why: When the cord was cut, a small stump was left. It fell off and left the belly button.

quiz.p: Which of these is true about families?
opts: Families are made in many ways, but every person began as one cell
Only families made by birth are real families
Adopted children began in a different way
quiz.why: Families can be made by birth, adoption and other ways. All are real. And every person, adopted or not, began as one cell and grew in a womb.

quiz.p: What do scientists still NOT fully know?
opts: How each cell knows exactly what to become
That babies grow in the womb
quiz.why: Scientists know a lot, but how millions of cells organise themselves into a body is still being worked out.

quiz.p: A baby in the womb hears which sounds best?
opts: Low sounds, like voices and the heartbeat
quiz.why: Low sounds travel through water and the body best. You can test this with a bag of water at your ear.

open_questions.q: How does each cell know exactly where it is and what to become?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know cells send chemical messages. But how millions of messages fit together into a whole, right-sized body is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: What starts birth? How does the body know the baby is ready?
open_questions.why_open: Signals from both the baby and the mother seem to matter. Scientists still do not know exactly which signal starts it, or why some babies come early.

open_questions.q: When does a growing baby begin to feel things, or be aware?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can ask a baby in the womb. Scientists argue about it, and different families and traditions also answer it differently.

open_questions.q: Why are human babies born so helpless, compared with calves or foals?
open_questions.why_open: Two main ideas compete: narrow hips and the mother's energy. There may be other reasons too.

open_questions.q: What do the baby's cells that stay in the mother's body actually do?
open_questions.why_open: They have been found in many parts of mothers' bodies, for decades. Some studies say they help heal, others link them to illness. Nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: How much does a baby learn and remember before it is born?
open_questions.why_open: Newborns know their mother's voice. But how much more they learn in the womb is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Why do some babies grow very well and others less, even with healthy mothers?
open_questions.why_open: Food, genes, the placenta and many other things all matter. How they work together is not fully known.

maths.problem: Remember the dough doubling, where one ball split into 2, then 4, then 8? If you keep going, how many balls after 6 rounds of splitting?
maths.explain: Each round doubles the number. 1, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. That is 6 rounds. So there are 64 balls.
maths.context: This is about the One Cell to Many activity, where you split a ball of dough again and again like a dividing cell.
maths.why_maths: Doubling is how cells grow in number. Seeing the pattern shows why one cell can become trillions.

maths.problem: A baby grows in the womb for about 40 weeks. There are 7 days in a week. About how many days is that?
maths.explain: 40 weeks times 7 days. 4 times 7 is 28. So 40 times 7 is 280. A baby grows for about 280 days.
maths.context: This is about the 40 weeks a baby grows in the womb, like the 40 squares in the Forty Weeks board game.
maths.why_maths: Doctors count in weeks, but we think in days and months. Multiplying turns one into the other.

maths.problem: In the Who Waits Longest? card game, an Indian elephant baby grows for about 650 days and a human baby for about 270 days. How many more days does the elephant baby grow?
maths.explain: 650 take away 270. 650 take away 200 is 450. Then 450 take away 70 is 380. So the elephant baby grows about 380 days longer.
maths.context: This is about the Who Waits Longest? card game, which compares how long different animal babies grow before birth.

chart.title: About how many days each baby grows inside its mother

maths.why_maths: A bar chart and a subtraction show how big the difference really is, not just which is longer.

maths.problem: On the fruit line, a newborn is about 50 centimetres long. You are now about 125 centimetres tall. How many newborn lengths tall are you?
maths.explain: Two newborns make 50 plus 50, which is 100 centimetres. That leaves 25 centimetres, which is half of 50. So you are 2 and a half newborn lengths tall.
maths.context: This is about How Big Was I?, where you marked a newborn's length of about 50 centimetres on a paper strip.
maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres lets you compare your size now with your size at birth exactly.

maths.problem: In Keep the Baby Warm, the bottle on a chest was 35 degrees after 20 minutes. The bottle alone was 29 degrees. How much warmer was the bottle on the chest?
maths.explain: 35 take away 29 is 6. So the bottle held on the chest stayed 6 degrees warmer than the bottle left alone.
maths.context: This is about Keep the Baby Warm. Three bottles of warm water were kept alone, wrapped, or held on a chest, and measured after 20 minutes. These numbers are made up as an example.
maths.why_maths: Reading a thermometer and finding the difference tells us how much kangaroo care helps, not just that it helps.

roots.context: We have been learning how a baby grows from one cell into a whole person. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You were never a separate thing that arrived. You grew out of another person, and out of the whole world, one cell at a time.
deep_truth.habit: We think of 'me' and 'my mother' or 'me' and 'the world' as two different things with a clear line between them. But for nine months your blood fed on hers, her food became your bones, and you began as a cell from each of two people. There was no moment when a finished 'you' was added from outside.
deep_truth.evidence: Every cell in you came from one first cell, built from food your mother ate, and a few of your cells may still live in her body.

three.who_am_i: You are a trillion cells that all came from one. You are one thing that became many.
three.what_is_life: Life is passed on, never started from nothing. Every living thing came from another living thing.
three.what_is_this_world: The rice, dal and sunlight your mother took in became you. The world is not around you. It is in you.

roots.thread: Before you, there was one cell. Before that, two cells from two people, each made from food, water, air and sunlight. DeepKids believes this is the One becoming the many: a single cell turns into skin, eyes, a beating heart and a mind that can wonder about it. Every one of your trillions of cells carries the same instructions, the same one, read in many ways. Nobody stops being part of the whole when they are born. They just begin to see it.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to split a tiny banyan seed. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all.' 'From that nothing you cannot see, this huge banyan tree grows. That is you.'
teachings.link: You began as one cell too small to see. Everything you are now grew out of it.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, the idea of 'interbeing'
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree inside it. Nothing exists all by itself.
teachings.link: Look deeply at a baby and you can see its mother's meals, the farmer's rice, the rain and the sun. A baby is made of everything.

teachings.teaching: The Tao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to all things.
teachings.link: One cell becomes two, two become four, and on and on, until there is a whole person.

science.text: Every cell in your body came from one first cell, and almost every one has the same DNA.
A few cells from a baby can live on in the mother's body for decades. What they do is not yet known.

other_view.who: Many biologists, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: A baby is a wonderful result of cells, chemistry and food. There is no deeper One inside it, and nothing more is needed to explain it. That is an honest and respectful view.
